claim: The restoration of homeostasis after tissue damage relies on proper spatial-temporal control of damage-induced apoptosis and compensatory proliferation.
source: The restoration of homeostasis after tissue damage relies on proper spatial-temporal control of damage-induced apoptosis and compensatory proliferation.
evidence: This is a general statement about tissue damage response presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this sentence, but is supported by the broader literature context.

claim: In Drosophila imaginal discs, damage-induced apoptosis and compensatory proliferation are coordinated by the stress response pathway JNK.
source: In Drosophila imaginal discs these processes are coordinated by the stress response pathway JNK.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental work presented in the manuscript and references to prior literature.

claim: JNK signaling induces a dose-dependent extension of G2 in tissue damage and tumors.
source: We demonstrate that JNK signaling induces a dose-dependent extension of G2 in tissue damage and tumors, resulting in either transient stalling or a prolonged but reversible cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through FUCCI reporter analysis, flow cytometry, and multiple experimental models shown in Figures 1-7.

claim: JNK-induced G2 extension results in either transient stalling or a prolonged but reversible cell cycle arrest.
source: We demonstrate that JNK signaling induces a dose-dependent extension of G2 in tissue damage and tumors, resulting in either transient stalling or a prolonged but reversible cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-course experiments showing recovery of cell cycle progression after JNK activity decreases (Figures 1, 2).

claim: G2-stalling is mediated by downregulation of the G2/M-specific phosphatase String(Stg)/Cdc25.
source: G2-stalling is mediated by downregulation of the G2/M-specific phosphatase String(Stg)/Cdc25.
evidence: This is supported by stg-GFP reporter downregulation in G2-arrested cells and rescue experiments with stg overexpression (Figure 4).

claim: Ectopic expression of stg is sufficient to suppress G2-stalling.
source: Ectopic expression of stg is sufficient to suppress G2-stalling and reveals roles for stalling in survival, proliferation and paracrine signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FUCCI analysis and EdU incorporation in egr,stg-coexpressing discs (Figure 4).

claim: G2-stalling protects cells from JNK-induced apoptosis.
source: G2-stalling protects cells from JNK-induced apoptosis, but under chronic conditions, reduces proliferative potential of JNK-signaling cells while promoting non-autonomous proliferation.
evidence: This is shown by increased apoptosis when stg is overexpressed to bypass G2-stalling in injured discs (Figure 6).

claim: Under chronic conditions, G2-stalling reduces proliferative potential of JNK-signaling cells.
source: G2-stalling protects cells from JNK-induced apoptosis, but under chronic conditions, reduces proliferative potential of JNK-signaling cells while promoting non-autonomous proliferation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by reduced regeneration in egr-expressing discs compared to improved regeneration when stg is overexpressed (Figure 5).

claim: Under chronic conditions, G2-stalling promotes non-autonomous proliferation.
source: G2-stalling protects cells from JNK-induced apoptosis, but under chronic conditions, reduces proliferative potential of JNK-signaling cells while promoting non-autonomous proliferation.
evidence: This is shown by reduced non-autonomous overgrowth when stg is overexpressed in tumor models (Figure 7).

claim: Transient cell cycle stalling in G2 has key roles in wound healing.
source: Thus, transient cell cycle stalling in G2 has key roles in wound healing but becomes detrimental upon chronic JNK overstimulation, with important implications for chronic wound healing pathologies or tumorigenic transformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the transient G2-shift observed in surgical injury models and its correlation with wound healing processes.

claim: Cell cycle stalling in G2 becomes detrimental upon chronic JNK overstimulation.
source: Thus, transient cell cycle stalling in G2 has key roles in wound healing but becomes detrimental upon chronic JNK overstimulation, with important implications for chronic wound healing pathologies or tumorigenic transformation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by poor regeneration in egr-expressing discs with chronic JNK activity and non-autonomous overgrowth in tumor models.

claim: Deregulation of injury-induced signals and cell behaviors are associated with ageing or pathologies, such as non-healing chronic wounds and cancer.
source: Accordingly, deregulation of injury-induced signals and cell behaviors are associated with ageing or pathologies, such as non-healing chronic wounds and cancer (Martin and Nunan, 2015; Neves et al., 2015; Taniguchi and Karin, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cell proliferation during tissue repair is regulated by controlling cell cycle progression, promoting re-entry of quiescent cells into the cell cycle or accelerating cell division rates.
source: Cell proliferation during tissue repair is regulated by controlling cell cycle progression, promoting re-entry of quiescent cells into the cell cycle or accelerating cell division rates.
evidence: This is a general statement about tissue repair mechanisms based on established knowledge.

claim: Tissue stress can induce cell cycle arrest.
source: In contrast to acceleration, tissue stress can also induce cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in the manuscript and established knowledge about stress responses.

claim: Excess cellular damage or deregulated signaling environments cause cells to arrest in G0 and enter senescence.
source: Excess cellular damage or deregulated signaling environments cause cells to arrest in G0 and enter senescence - a state characterized by resistance to apoptosis and senescence-associated secretory phenotypes (SASP) (Hernandez-Segura et al., 2018; Neves et al., 2015; Pluquet et al., 2015; Salama et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature on senescence.

claim: Senescence is characterized by resistance to apoptosis and senescence-associated secretory phenotypes (SASP).
source: Excess cellular damage or deregulated signaling environments cause cells to arrest in G0 and enter senescence - a state characterized by resistance to apoptosis and senescence-associated secretory phenotypes (SASP) (Hernandez-Segura et al., 2018; Neves et al., 2015; Pluquet et al., 2015; Salama et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on senescence characteristics.

claim: SASP is linked to persistent production of signaling molecules, secretion of ECM degrading enzymes, as well as an upregulation of autophagy, unfolded protein response (UPR), ROS and an increase in cell size.
source: SASP is linked to persistent production of signaling molecules, secretion of ECM degrading enzymes, as well as an upregulation of autophagy, unfolded protein response (UPR), ROS and an increase in cell size (Hernandez-Segura et al., 2018; Neves et al., 2015; Pluquet et al., 2015; Salama et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on SASP characteristics.

claim: Senescent cells are required at wound sites to promote wound closure and cell plasticity.
source: Strikingly, recent studies suggest that senescent cells are required at wound sites to promote wound closure and cell plasticity (Demaria et al., 2014; Ritschka et al., 2017) and in development to promote morphogenesis of embryonic structures (Davaapil et al., 2017; Muñoz-Espín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on senescent cells in wound healing.

claim: Senescent cells are required in development to promote morphogenesis of embryonic structures.
source: Strikingly, recent studies suggest that senescent cells are required at wound sites to promote wound closure and cell plasticity (Demaria et al., 2014; Ritschka et al., 2017) and in development to promote morphogenesis of embryonic structures (Davaapil et al., 2017; Muñoz-Espín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on senescent cells in development.

claim: The JNK/MAPK-cascade is among the earliest pathways activated by physical wounding.
source: The JNK/MAPK-cascade is among the earliest pathways activated by physical wounding (Bosch et al., 2005; Rämet et al., 2002), loss of epithelial polarity (Igaki, 2009; Igaki, 2009) or apoptosis (Ryoo et al., 2004; Shlevkov and Morata, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on JNK activation.

claim: The JNK/MAPK-cascade is among the earliest pathways activated by loss of epithelial polarity.
source: The JNK/MAPK-cascade is among the earliest pathways activated by physical wounding (Bosch et al., 2005; Rämet et al., 2002), loss of epithelial polarity (Igaki, 2009; Igaki, 2009) or apoptosis (Ryoo et al., 2004; Shlevkov and Morata, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on JNK activation.

claim: The JNK/MAPK-cascade is among the earliest pathways activated by apoptosis.
source: The JNK/MAPK-cascade is among the earliest pathways activated by physical wounding (Bosch et al., 2005; Rämet et al., 2002), loss of epithelial polarity (Igaki, 2009; Igaki, 2009) or apoptosis (Ryoo et al., 2004; Shlevkov and Morata, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on JNK activation.

claim: JNK activates multiple transcription factors, such as AP-1.
source: JNK activates multiple transcription factors, such as AP-1 (Eferl and Wagner, 2003; Külshammer et al., 2015), and is required for wound closure (Bosch et al., 2005; Ríos-Barrera and Riesgo-Escovar, 2013), elimination of damaged cells (Chen, 2012; Moreno et al., 2002; Shlevkov and Morata, 2012) and compensatory proliferation replacing lost tissues (Bergantiños et al., 2010; Bosch et al., 2008; Ryoo et al., 2004; Sun and Irvine, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on JNK signaling.

claim: JNK is required for wound closure.
source: JNK activates multiple transcription factors, such as AP-1 (Eferl and Wagner, 2003; Külshammer et al., 2015), and is required for wound closure (Bosch et al., 2005; Ríos-Barrera and Riesgo-Escovar, 2013), elimination of damaged cells (Chen, 2012; Moreno et al., 2002; Shlevkov and Morata, 2012) and compensatory proliferation replacing lost tissues (Bergantiños et al., 2010; Bosch et al., 2008; Ryoo et al., 2004; Sun and Irvine, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on JNK function.

claim: JNK is required for elimination of damaged cells.
source: JNK activates multiple transcription factors, such as AP-1 (Eferl and Wagner, 2003; Külshammer et al., 2015), and is required for wound closure (Bosch et al., 2005; Ríos-Barrera and Riesgo-Escovar, 2013), elimination of damaged cells (Chen, 2012; Moreno et al., 2002; Shlevkov and Morata, 2012) and compensatory proliferation replacing lost tissues (Bergantiños et al., 2010; Bosch et al., 2008; Ryoo et al., 2004; Sun and Irvine, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on JNK function.

claim: JNK is required for compensatory proliferation replacing lost tissues.
source: JNK activates multiple transcription factors, such as AP-1 (Eferl and Wagner, 2003; Külshammer et al., 2015), and is required for wound closure (Bosch et al., 2005; Ríos-Barrera and Riesgo-Escovar, 2013), elimination of damaged cells (Chen, 2012; Moreno et al., 2002; Shlevkov and Morata, 2012) and compensatory proliferation replacing lost tissues (Bergantiños et al., 2010; Bosch et al., 2008; Ryoo et al., 2004; Sun and Irvine, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on JNK function.

claim: Feed-back loops acting through ROS, p53 and the initiator caspase Dronc maintain JNK activity until tissue homeostasis is restored.
source: Feed-back loops acting through ROS, p53 and the initiator caspase Dronc maintain JNK activity until tissue homeostasis is restored (Brock et al., 2017; Khan et al., 2017; Shlevkov and Morata, 2012; Wells et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on JNK regulation.

claim: Apoptotic cells stimulate compensatory proliferation of the surrounding tissue by JNK-dependent activation of growth and survival pathways including Hippo/Yorkie and JAK/STAT.
source: Apoptotic cells stimulate compensatory proliferation of the surrounding tissue by JNK-dependent activation of growth and survival pathways including Hippo/Yorkie and JAK/STAT (Fuchs and Steller, 2015; Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2013; Sun and Irvine, 2011; Zielke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on compensatory proliferation.

claim: Preventing execution of apoptosis in damaged, aberrant or tumorigenic cells causes chronic signaling and non-autonomous overgrowth in fly tissues.
source: Importantly, preventing execution of apoptosis in damaged, aberrant or tumorigenic cells causes chronic signaling and non-autonomous overgrowth in fly tissues (Fuchs and Steller, 2015; Herz et al., 2006; Martín et al., 2009; Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2013; Pérez-Garijo et al., 2004; Pérez-Garijo et al., 2009; Ryoo et al., 2004; Uhlirova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on apoptosis and overgrowth.

claim: Activation of the JNK reporter puc-LacZ was observed near the wound site 6 hr post-injury.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Bosch et al., 2005; Mattila et al., 2005; Rämet et al., 2002), we observed activation of the JNK reporter puc-LacZ near the wound site 6 hr post-injury (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1A-B and is consistent with prior reports.

claim: Upregulation of the JNK reporter coincided with a pronounced shift of cells towards a G2-dominated cell cycle profile.
source: Strikingly, upregulation of the JNK reporter coincided with a pronounced shift of cells towards a G2-dominated cell cycle profile visualized by the G2-specific FUCCI reporter mRFP-NLS-CycB1-266 (Figure 1A',B'; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) (Zielke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1A',B' using FUCCI reporters.

claim: Cells from injured imaginal discs positive for the JNK-reporter TRE-RFP exhibited a pronounced G2-shift by flow cytometry.
source: We confirmed this finding by flow cytometry, where cells from injured imaginal discs positive for the alternative JNK-reporter TRE-RFP (Chatterjee and Bohmann, 2012) exhibited a pronounced G2-shift (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1D,E by flow cytometry analysis.

claim: Injury-induced JNK-activity and the G2-profile were transient events, as both decreased by 16 hr post-injury.
source: Importantly, injury-induced JNK-activity and the G2-profile were transient events, as both decreased by 16 hr post-injury (Figure 1C,C').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1C,C' by time-course analysis.

claim: JNK activity correlates with a G2 cell cycle profile and this correlation may be a transient component of physiological wound healing processes.
source: These observations suggest that JNK activity correlates with a G2 cell cycle profile and that this correlation may be a transient component of physiological wound healing processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the transient nature of both JNK activity and G2-shift in surgical injury experiments.

claim: Expression of TNFα/eiger under the control of rnGAL4 results in extensive cell death and reduced adult wing sizes.
source: As described previously, we observed extensive cell death resulting in reduced adult wing sizes (Herrera et al., 2013; La Fortezza et al., 2016; Smith-Bolton et al., 2009) and broad activation of the JNK-reporter TRE-RFP in and around egr-expressing cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C) (La Fortezza et al., 2016).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with prior reports.

claim: Expression of eiger results in broad activation of the JNK-reporter TRE-RFP in and around egr-expressing cells.
source: As described previously, we observed extensive cell death resulting in reduced adult wing sizes (Herrera et al., 2013; La Fortezza et al., 2016; Smith-Bolton et al., 2009) and broad activation of the JNK-reporter TRE-RFP in and around egr-expressing cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C) (La Fortezza et al., 2016).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: FUCCI assays revealed a pronounced G2-shift of cells at the center of egr-expressing domains.
source: Importantly, FUCCI assays revealed a pronounced G2-shift of cells at the center of egr-expressing domains (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2A,B using FUCCI reporters.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis confirmed that cells positive for TRE-RFP exhibit a pronounced G2-profile.
source: Flow cytometry analysis confirmed that cells positive for TRE-RFP (Figure 2C,C'), and particularly the GFP-labeled lineage of egr-expressing cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B',C'), exhibit a pronounced G2-profile.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2C,C' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B',C' by flow cytometry.

claim: DNA replication activity and mitotic cells were absent from G2-shifted, TRE-positive domains in egr-expressing discs.
source: EdU incorporation assays (Figure 2A,B,D) and staining for phospho-Histone 3 (pH3) (Figure 2E,F) revealed that DNA replication activity and mitotic cells were absent from G2-shifted, TRE-positive domains in egr-expressing discs.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2A,B,D,E,F by EdU incorporation and pH3 staining.

claim: TRE-positive G2 cells were larger in size than G2 cells from undamaged control discs.
source: Of note, TRE-positive G2 cells were larger in size than G2 cells from undamaged control discs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D by flow cytometry analysis of cell size.

claim: The G2 profile in egr-expressing discs represents a cell cycle arrest.
source: Combined, these observations confirm a pronounced correlation between injury-induced JNK activity and a G2-dominated cell cycle observed in surgically injured discs and suggest that the G2 profile represents a cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of DNA replication and mitotic activity in G2-shifted cells.

claim: JNK-arrested cells resume mitotic activity and cellular growth during the recovery period after egr-expression ceases.
source: To independently confirm that G2-arrested cells resume mitotic activity and cellular growth, we analyzed how JNK and cell cycle activity changed during the recovery period.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FUCCI and EdU incorporation assays at different recovery time points (Figure 2G-K').

claim: At 24 hr into the recovery period, egr-expressing discs showed decreasing but still pronounced JNK activity.
source: When we analyzed TRE-activity in egr-expressing discs at 24 hr into the recovery period, we observed decreasing but still pronounced JNK activity (Figure 2G-H').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2G-H' by TRE-RFP reporter analysis.

claim: At 24 hr into the recovery period, FUCCI analysis and EdU incorporation indicated the presence of G2 cells but also of isolated events of DNA replication activity at the center of the pouch.
source: FUCCI analysis and EdU incorporation indicated the presence of G2 cells but also of isolated events of DNA replication activity at the center of the pouch (Figure 2J,J').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2J,J' by FUCCI and EdU analysis.

claim: At 72 hr into the recovery period, TRE-reporter activity was strongly reduced.
source: However, 72 hr into the recovery period, TRE-reporter activity was strongly reduced (Figure 2I,I'), and FUCCI as well as EdU incorporation assays revealed actively cycling cells (Figure 2K,K').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2I,I' by TRE-RFP reporter analysis.

claim: At 72 hr into the recovery period, FUCCI and EdU incorporation assays revealed actively cycling cells.
source: However, 72 hr into the recovery period, TRE-reporter activity was strongly reduced (Figure 2I,I'), and FUCCI as well as EdU incorporation assays revealed actively cycling cells (Figure 2K,K').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2K,K' by FUCCI and EdU analysis.

claim: JNK-induced stalling of the cell cycle in G2 is reversible.
source: Combined, these results suggest that JNK-induced stalling of the cell cycle in G2 is reversible.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the recovery of cell cycle activity after JNK activity decreases.

claim: TRE-reporter activity scaled with the proportion of cells in G2 and also with stalling-associated increase in cell size.
source: Specifically, TRE-reporter activity scaled with the proportion of cells in G2 and also with stalling-associated increase in cell size (Figure 2L,L').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2L,L' by flow cytometry analysis.

claim: Injury-induced stalling of cells in G2 represents a dose-dependent response to spatio-temporal JNK activity.
source: We thus suggest that injury-induced stalling of cells in G2 represent a dose-dependent response to spatio-temporal JNK activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between TRE-reporter activity levels and G2-stalling.

claim: Transient expression of constitutively active JNKK Hemipterous (hepACT) in the disc pouch induces a cell cycle shift towards G2 and absence of DNA replication.
source: To test this hypothesis, we transiently expressed a constitutively active form of JNKK Hemipterous (hepACT) in the disc pouch using rnGAL4. FUCCI analysis indeed revealed a cell cycle shift towards G2 and absence of DNA replication (Figure 3A,A'), indicating that JNK is sufficient to induce G2-stalling.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3A,A' by FUCCI and EdU analysis.

claim: JNK is sufficient to induce G2-stalling.
source: FUCCI analysis indeed revealed a cell cycle shift towards G2 and absence of DNA replication (Figure 3A,A'), indicating that JNK is sufficient to induce G2-stalling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by hepACT expression experiments shown in Figure 3A,A'.

claim: Inhibition of JNK blocked upregulation of the JNK-reporter puc-LacZ in the posterior compartment of injured discs.
source: As expected, inhibition of JNK blocked upregulation of the JNK-reporter puc-LacZ in the posterior compartment of injured discs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3B by puc-LacZ reporter analysis in bskDN-expressing discs.

claim: Inhibition of JNK prevented a cell cycle shift towards G2 at the site of injury.
source: Importantly, it also prevented a cell cycle shift towards G2 at the site of injury (Figure 3B').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3B' by FUCCI analysis in bskDN-expressing injured discs.

claim: JNK-signaling in response to tissue damage is sufficient and necessary to induce G2-stalling.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that JNK-signaling in response to tissue damage is sufficient and necessary to induce G2-stalling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by both gain-of-function (hepACT) and loss-of-function (bskDN) experiments.

claim: JNK signaling in the wing peripodium is required for wing eversion at the larval-pupal transition.
source: JNK in the wing peripodium is required for disc eversion (Pastor-Pareja et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: TRE activity in the peripodium correlated with a G2 profile and absence of DNA replication.
source: Strikingly, TRE activity in the peripodium correlated with a G2 profile and absence of DNA replication (Figure 3C, C', Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,A').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3C,C' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,A' by TRE-RFP, FUCCI, and EdU analysis.

claim: The peripodium of size-matched hepR75 discs displayed a significant reduction in the number of G2 cells and an increase in G1-phase cells, if compared to wild type discs.
source: Indeed, the peripodium of size-matched hepR75 discs displayed a significant reduction in the number of G2 cells and an increase in G1-phase cells, if compared to wild type discs (Figure 3D-G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-E).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3D-G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-E by FUCCI analysis in hepR75 mutant discs.

claim: JNK is at least partially necessary for developmentally regulated G2-stalling in the absence of tissue damage.
source: Combined, these observations indicate that JNK is at least partially necessary for one example of developmentally regulated G2-stalling in the absence of tissue damage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reduction in G2 cells in hepR75 mutant peripodium.

claim: There is no correlation between the occurrence of ɣH2Av and G2-stalling in egr-expressing discs.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, we observed no correlation between the occurrence of ɣH2Av, a marker of dsDNA breaks (Khurana and Oberdoerffer, 2015), and G2-stalling in egr-expressing discs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-A'').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-A'' by ɣH2Av staining and FUCCI analysis.

claim: Knock-down of chk1 (grp) did not prevent the appearance of a G2-dominated FUCCI profile in egr-expressing discs.
source: Moreover, neither knock-down of the DNA damage sensing and relay components chk1 (grp), ATR (mei-41), nor organismal hemizygosity for mei-41RT1 prevented the appearance of a G2-dominated FUCCI profile in egr-expressing discs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B by FUCCI analysis in egr,grp RNAi-expressing discs.

claim: Knock-down of ATR (mei-41) did not prevent the appearance of a G2-dominated FUCCI profile in egr-expressing discs.
source: Moreover, neither knock-down of the DNA damage sensing and relay components chk1 (grp), ATR (mei-41), nor organismal hemizygosity for mei-41RT1 prevented the appearance of a G2-dominated FUCCI profile in egr-expressing discs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C by FUCCI analysis in egr,mei-41 RNAi-expressing discs.

claim: Organismal hemizygosity for mei-41RT1 did not prevent the appearance of a G2-dominated FUCCI profile in egr-expressing discs.
source: Moreover, neither knock-down of the DNA damage sensing and relay components chk1 (grp), ATR (mei-41), nor organismal hemizygosity for mei-41RT1 prevented the appearance of a G2-dominated FUCCI profile in egr-expressing discs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D by FUCCI analysis in mei-41RT1 hemizygous, egr-expressing discs.

claim: DNA damage per se is not a rate-limiting driver of G2-stalling.
source: We conclude that DNA damage per se, normally a potent inducer of G2/M arrests (Sancar et al., 2004; Song, 2005), is not a rate-limiting driver of G2-stalling.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between DNA damage markers and G2-stalling, and the inability of DNA damage pathway inhibition to prevent G2-stalling.

claim: Knock-down of Cdk1 in the wing pouch induced a dramatic shift of the FUCCI profile, resembling the shift observed in egr-expressing discs.
source: Knock-down of Cdk1 in the wing pouch induced a dramatic shift of the FUCCI profile, resembling the shift observed in egr-expressing discs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B by FUCCI analysis in Cdk1 RNAi-expressing discs.

claim: A lack of Cdk1 activity may arrest JNK-signaling cells.
source: This suggests that a lack of Cdk1 activity may arrest JNK-signaling cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between Cdk1 knockdown and egr-induced G2-stalling.

claim: A rate limiting activator of Cdk1 during the G2/M transition is the Cdc25-type phosphatase String (Stg).
source: A rate limiting activator of Cdk1 during the G2/M transition is the Cdc25-type phosphatase String (Stg) (Edgar et al., 2001; Kimelman, 2014; Kiyokawa and Ray, 2008), whose proteasomal degradation is regulated by Tribbles (Trbl) (Mata et al., 2000; Seher and Leptin, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on cell cycle regulation.

claim: Proteasomal degradation of String is regulated by Tribbles (Trbl).
source: A rate limiting activator of Cdk1 during the G2/M transition is the Cdc25-type phosphatase String (Stg) (Edgar et al., 2001; Kimelman, 2014; Kiyokawa and Ray, 2008), whose proteasomal degradation is regulated by Tribbles (Trbl) (Mata et al., 2000; Seher and Leptin, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on cell cycle regulation.

claim: Expression of the stg-GFP trap was dramatically downregulated in G2-shifted cells of egr-expressing discs.
source: We observed that expression of the stg-GFP trap was dramatically downregulated in G2-shifted cells of egr-expressing discs (Figure 4A-B') suggesting that stg transcription was reduced.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4A-B' by stg-GFP reporter analysis.

claim: stg transcription was reduced in G2-shifted cells of egr-expressing discs.
source: We observed that expression of the stg-GFP trap was dramatically downregulated in G2-shifted cells of egr-expressing discs (Figure 4A-B') suggesting that stg transcription was reduced.
evidence: This is inferred from the downregulation of the stg-GFP transcriptional reporter.

claim: A GFP-tagged Tribbles protein was highly upregulated in egr-expressing and surgically injured discs.
source: A GFP-tagged Tribbles protein (Nagarkar-Jaiswal et al., 2015; Otsuki and Brand, 2018) was highly upregulated in egr-expressing and surgically injured discs (Figure 4C-E) in a manner that was dependent on JNK activity (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4C-E by Trbl-GFP analysis.

claim: Upregulation of Tribbles-GFP in egr-expressing and surgically injured discs was dependent on JNK activity.
source: A GFP-tagged Tribbles protein (Nagarkar-Jaiswal et al., 2015; Otsuki and Brand, 2018) was highly upregulated in egr-expressing and surgically injured discs (Figure 4C-E) in a manner that was dependent on JNK activity (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4E by Trbl-GFP analysis in bskDN-expressing injured discs.

claim: JNK-activity separately impinges on stg transcription and Trbl availability, potentially underlying stalling of cells in G2 in parallel pathways.
source: Thus, JNK-activity seperately impinges on stg transcription and Trbl availability, potentially underlying stalling of cells in G2 in parallel pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the separate regulation of stg and Trbl by JNK.

claim: Overexpression of stg in egr-expressing cells re-established a heterogeneous FUCCI cell cycle profile.
source: Importantly, overexpression of stg and or knockdown of trbl in egr-expressing cells re-established a heterogeneous FUCCI cell cycle profile (Figure 4F-H).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4F-H by FUCCI analysis in egr,stg-coexpressing discs.

claim: Knockdown of trbl in egr-expressing cells re-established a heterogeneous FUCCI cell cycle profile.
source: Importantly, overexpression of stg and or knockdown of trbl in egr-expressing cells re-established a heterogeneous FUCCI cell cycle profile (Figure 4F-H).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4F-H by FUCCI analysis in egr,trbl RNAi-coexpressing discs.

claim: Cycling cells in egr,stg-coexpressing domains could be detected by EdU incorporation and pH3 labeling.
source: Specifically, cycling cells in egr,stg-coexpressing domains could be detected by EdU incorporation and pH3 labeling (Figure 4I-J').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 4I-J' by EdU and pH3 analysis.

claim: trbl and stg are rate limiting for cell cycle progression in JNK-signaling cells.
source: Combined, these observations suggest that trbl and stg are rate limiting for cell cycle progression in JNK-signaling cells and that overexpression of stg or knockdown of trbl is sufficient to override damage-induced cell cycle stalling in G2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the rescue of cell cycle progression when stg is overexpressed or trbl is knocked down.

claim: Overexpression of stg or knockdown of trbl is sufficient to override damage-induced cell cycle stalling in G2.
source: Combined, these observations suggest that trbl and stg are rate limiting for cell cycle progression in JNK-signaling cells and that overexpression of stg or knockdown of trbl is sufficient to override damage-induced cell cycle stalling in G2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the rescue of cell cycle progression when stg is overexpressed or trbl is knocked down.

claim: egr-expressing discs normally present with a folded architecture.
source: egr-expressing discs normally present with a folded architecture (Figure 5A,B) and large G2-arrested cells at the center of the pouch (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5A,B by tissue morphology analysis.

claim: egr,stg-co-expressing discs presented with densely and regularly arranged columnar cells.
source: In contrast, egr,stg-co-expressing discs presented with densely and regularly arranged columnar cells (Figure 5A-C').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5A-C' by tissue morphology analysis.

claim: stg co-expression improved tissue regeneration in egr-expressing discs, as assessed by size and morphology of adult wings.
source: Moreover, stg co-expression improved tissue regeneration in egr-expressing discs, as assessed by size and morphology of adult wings.
evidence: This is demonstrated by adult wing size analysis shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: 59% of adult wings developing from egr,stg-co-expressing discs were of wild type size, in contrast to just 14% of wings developing from egr-expressing discs.
source: 59% of adult wings developing from egr,stg-co-expressing discs were of wild type size, in contrast to just 14% of wings developing from egr-expressing discs (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5E by adult wing size quantification.

claim: stg expression did not interfere with activation of apoptosis in response to egr expression.
source: Importantly, stg expression did not interfere with activation of apoptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-G) or JNK activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H) in response to egr expression.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-G by Dcp-1 staining.

claim: stg expression did not interfere with JNK activation in response to egr expression.
source: Importantly, stg expression did not interfere with activation of apoptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-G) or JNK activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H) in response to egr expression.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H by TRE-RFP quantification.

claim: The egr,stg-expressing cell population labelled by G-TRACE was larger in size than egr-expressing population.
source: Instead, the egr,stg-expressing cell population labelled by G-TRACE (Evans et al., 2009) was larger in size (Figure 5F-H).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5F-H by G-TRACE lineage analysis.

claim: stg overexpression did not interfere with cell ablation but specifically with arrest of the cell cycle and thus proliferative capacity in egr-expressing cells.
source: This suggests that stg overexpression did not interfere with cell ablation but specifically with arrest of the cell cycle and thus proliferative capacity in egr-expressing cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that stg overexpression improves regeneration without affecting apoptosis or JNK activation.

claim: egr-expressing discs exhibit low regenerative potential, in contrast to discs expressing the pro-apoptotic gene hid.
source: egr-expressing discs had been previously reported to exhibit low regenerative potential, in contrast to discs expressing the pro-apoptotic gene hid (Herrera et al., 2013), an antagonist of Diap1-dependent inhibition of caspase activity (Vaux and Silke, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Preventing a G2-arrest in egr-expressing discs by stg overexpression phenocopied hid-induced regeneration.
source: Strikingly, preventing a G2-arrest in egr-expressing discs by stg overexpression phenocopied hid-induced regeneration, where discs display columnar morphology (Figure 5D,D') and regenerate efficiently to normal-sized adult wings (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of egr,stg and hid-expressing discs in Figure 5.

claim: hid-expressing discs display columnar morphology.
source: Strikingly, preventing a G2-arrest in egr-expressing discs by stg overexpression phenocopied hid-induced regeneration, where discs display columnar morphology (Figure 5D,D') and regenerate efficiently to normal-sized adult wings (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5D,D' by tissue morphology analysis.

claim: hid-expressing discs regenerate efficiently to normal-sized adult wings.
source: Strikingly, preventing a G2-arrest in egr-expressing discs by stg overexpression phenocopied hid-induced regeneration, where discs display columnar morphology (Figure 5D,D') and regenerate efficiently to normal-sized adult wings (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C by adult wing size analysis.

claim: hid-expressing discs activated the TRE-reporter only at low levels.
source: Importantly, hid-expressing discs activated the TRE-reporter only at low levels and forwent the pronounced changes to FUCCI reporter activity observed in egr-expressing discs (Figure 5I-L).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5I-L by TRE-RFP and FUCCI analysis.

claim: hid-expressing discs forwent the pronounced changes to FUCCI reporter activity observed in egr-expressing discs.
source: Importantly, hid-expressing discs activated the TRE-reporter only at low levels and forwent the pronounced changes to FUCCI reporter activity observed in egr-expressing discs (Figure 5I-L).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5I-L by FUCCI analysis.

claim: Persistent stalling and arrest of cells in G2 interferes with regeneration in egr-expressing discs by interfering with the ability of cells to divide and proliferate.
source: These observations indicate that persistent stalling and arrest of cells in G2 interferes with regeneration in egr-expressing discs by interfering with the ability of cells to divide and proliferate.
evidence: This is inferred from the improved regeneration when G2-stalling is bypassed by stg overexpression.

claim: G2-stalling is a dose-sensitive JNK-effector which determines the regenerative potential of different experimental regeneration models.
source: Moreover, they highlight G2-stalling as dose-sensitive JNK-effector which determines the regenerative potential of different experimental regeneration models.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of egr and hid models with different levels of JNK activity and regenerative capacity.

claim: egr-expression induced TRE-reporter activity at much higher levels and at longer timescales than surgical injury.
source: Of note, egr-expression also induced TRE-reporter activity at much higher levels (Figure 7B,B',D,D') and at longer timescales than surgical injury (Figure 5M,N), supporting our conclusion that egr-expressing discs may experience extreme and possibly aberrant G2 stalling and arrest.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 5M,N and Figure 7B,B',D,D' by TRE-RFP quantification.

claim: 6 hr after injury, there was a 2-fold increase in the apoptotic domain within injured discs when stg was overexpressed.
source: Strikingly, 6 hr after injury, we observed a 2-fold increase in the apoptotic domain within injured discs (Figure 6A-E).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6A-E by Dcp-1 quantification in stg-overexpressing injured discs.

claim: While stg overexpression induced apoptosis primarily at the anterior D/V boundary in undamaged control discs, apoptosis in surgically injured discs was specifically increased near the wound site where JNK reporters are expected to be activated.
source: Importantly, while stg overexpression also induced apoptosis primarily at the anterior D/V boundary in undamaged control discs, apoptosis in surgically injured discs was specifically increased near the wound site where JNK reporters are expected to be activated (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6B,D by Dcp-1 staining patterns.

claim: At transient time scales, G2-stalling is required to prevent apoptosis and thus promotes survival in injured tissues displaying potentially lethal levels of JNK activity.
source: This suggests that at transient time scales, G2-stalling is required to prevent apoptosis and thus promotes survival in injured tissues displaying potentially lethal levels of JNK activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased apoptosis when G2-stalling is bypassed in injured discs.

claim: In actively cycling, JNK-signaling tissue, Dcp-1 could be specifically detected in cells with low intensity of either FUCCI reporter.
source: We found that in actively cycling, JNK-signaling tissue, Dcp-1 could be specifically detected in cells with low intensity of either FUCCI reporter (Figure 6F-G'), suggesting that JNK-signaling cells preferentially died either early in G1 or late in S-phase.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6F-G' by correlation of Dcp-1 with FUCCI reporter intensities.

claim: JNK-signaling cells preferentially died either early in G1 or late in S-phase.
source: We found that in actively cycling, JNK-signaling tissue, Dcp-1 could be specifically detected in cells with low intensity of either FUCCI reporter (Figure 6F-G'), suggesting that JNK-signaling cells preferentially died either early in G1 or late in S-phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation of Dcp-1 with low FUCCI reporter intensities.

claim: Low FUCCI reporter fluorescence was not due to apoptosis-dependent degradation of fluorophores.
source: Importantly, low FUCCI reporter fluorescence was not due to apoptosis-dependent degradation of fluorophores, as levels of fluorescence intensity of an unrelated cytoplasmic GFP were independent of Dcp-1 levels in egr,GFP-co-expressing discs (Figure 6H-I).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6H-I by correlation of free GFP with Dcp-1 levels.

claim: JNK-signaling cells are susceptible to apoptosis in G1 and protected from apoptosis by stalling in G2.
source: Taken together, these results support a model where JNK-signaling cells are susceptible to apoptosis in G1 and protected from apoptosis by stalling in G2.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle phase-specific apoptosis patterns observed.

claim: A Hid-GFP fusion protein expressed under the control of endogenous regulatory elements was strongly upregulated in TRE-positive cells in egr-expressing discs.
source: A Hid-GFP fusion protein expressed under the control of endogenous regulatory elements (Nagarkar-Jaiswal et al., 2015) was also strongly upregulated in TRE-positive cells in egr-expressing discs (Figure 6L-M').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 6L-M' by Hid-GFP analysis.

claim: Activation of anti-apoptotic and pro-apoptotic pathways occurs concomitantly in JNK-signaling G2-stalled cells.
source: We highlight that the activation of anti-apoptotic and pro-apoptotic pathways occurs concomitantly in JNK-signaling G2-stalled cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simultaneous upregulation of Diap1 and Hid in G2-stalled cells.

claim: Transition from G2 to G1 represents the key switch in the cellular interpretation of opposing JNK-dependent signals with anti-apoptotic to pro-apoptotic consequences.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that transition from G2 to G1 represents the key switch in the cellular interpretation of opposing JNK-dependent signals with anti-apoptotic to pro-apoptotic consequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle phase-specific survival and apoptosis patterns.

claim: Cell cycle arrest and apoptosis resistance are hallmarks of senescence.
source: Cell cycle arrest and apoptosis resistance are hallmarks of senescence.
evidence: This is established knowledge about senescence characteristics.

claim: Senescent cells affect their microenvironment through senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).
source: Senescent cells affect their microenvironment through senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) (Hernandez-Segura et al., 2018; Neves et al., 2015; Pluquet et al., 2015; Salama et al., 2014), which promotes tumorigenesis and contributes to tumor heterogeneity (Hinds and Pietruska, 2017; Schosserer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on senescence.

claim: SASP promotes tumorigenesis and contributes to tumor heterogeneity.
source: Senescent cells affect their microenvironment through senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) (Hernandez-Segura et al., 2018; Neves et al., 2015; Pluquet et al., 2015; Salama et al., 2014), which promotes tumorigenesis and contributes to tumor heterogeneity (Hinds and Pietruska, 2017; Schosserer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on SASP and cancer.

claim: Many studies report heterogenous activation of JNK in imaginal discs upon genetic loss of tumor suppressor function.
source: Many studies report heterogenous activation of JNK in imaginal discs upon genetic loss of tumor suppressor function (Richardson and Portela, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior review.

claim: 40.6% of wtsx1 cells had at least elevated TRE-RFP reporter activity based on flow cytometry analysis.
source: Based on flow cytometry analysis, we estimated that 40.6% of wtsx1 cells had at least elevated TRE-RFP reporter activity.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data from wtsx1 mosaic discs.

claim: 29.9% of wild type cells displayed TRE-RFP reporter activity in wtsx1 mosaic discs.
source: Consistent with non-autonomous induction of JNK in response to tissue stress (Bosch et al., 2005; Herrera et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2010) 29.9% of wild type cells displayed TRE-RFP reporter activity.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data from wtsx1 mosaic discs and is consistent with prior reports of non-autonomous JNK activation.

claim: TRE-RFP levels in wtsx1 mosaic discs were comparable to levels induced by surgical injury but much lower than those induced by egr-expression.
source: Importantly, TRE-RFP levels were comparable to levels induced by surgical injury but much lower than those induced by egr-expression (Figure 7B-D').
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7B-D' by TRE-RFP comparison across different models.

claim: TRE-positive cells in wtsx1 mosaic discs exhibited a strong G2 profile which correlated with an increase in cell size.
source: Flow cytometry analysis revealed that TRE-positive cells exhibited a strong G2 profile which correlated with an increase in cell size (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7E,F by flow cytometry analysis.

claim: The relationship between TRE-positivity, G2 profile, and increased cell size could also be observed in mosaic discs containing clones mutant for scribdt12.
source: This relationship could also be observed in mosaic discs containing clones mutant for scribdt12, a hypomorphic tumor suppressor mutation in the key component of the Scrib/Lgl/Dlg epithelial polarity module (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-D) (Stephens et al., 2018; Zeitler et al., 2004).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-D by flow cytometry analysis of scribdt12 mosaic discs.

claim: A pronounced shift towards G2 is associated with JNK activity in response to tissue stress imposed by the presence of abnormal or tumorigenic cells.
source: Combined, these observations suggest that a pronounced shift towards G2 is associated with JNK activity in response to tissue stress imposed by the presence of abnormal or tumorigenic cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the G2-shift observed in tumor models with JNK activity.

claim: stg overexpression in wtsx1 and in dlg1G0342 cells strongly affected the surrounding wild type tissue.
source: Strikingly, however, when we further analyzed these mosaic discs, we found that stg overexpression in wtsx1 and in dlg1G0342 cells strongly affected the surrounding wild type tissue.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of wild type tissue volume in mosaic discs.

claim: Mitotic activity in wtsx1 clones was unaffected by stg overexpression.
source: Importantly, whereas mitotic activity in wtsx1 clones was unaffected (Figure 7L), stg-overexpression strongly reduced mitotic activity in the wild type tissue surrounding wtsx1 clones (Figure 7M).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7L by pH3 quantification in wtsx1 clones.

claim: stg-overexpression strongly reduced mitotic activity in the wild type tissue surrounding wtsx1 clones.
source: Importantly, whereas mitotic activity in wtsx1 clones was unaffected (Figure 7L), stg-overexpression strongly reduced mitotic activity in the wild type tissue surrounding wtsx1 clones (Figure 7M).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7M by pH3 quantification in wild type tissue.

claim: Stalling of JNK-signaling cells in G2 directly promotes non-autonomous proliferation and thus causes non-autonomous overgrowth on prolonged timescales during imaginal disc tumor development.
source: This strongly suggests that stalling of JNK-signaling cells in G2 directly promotes non-autonomous proliferation and thus causes non-autonomous overgrowth on prolonged timescales during imaginal disc tumor development.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in non-autonomous overgrowth when G2-stalling is bypassed in tumor models.

claim: Undead cells are created by expression of the anti-apoptotic factor p35 in apoptotic JNK-signaling cells.
source: Previous studies describe 'undead' cells as chronic drivers of non-autonomous overgrowth. Experimentally, undead cells are created by expression the anti-apoptotic factor p35 in apoptotic JNK-signaling cells (Chen, 2012; Fuchs and Steller, 2015; Martín et al., 2009; Pérez-Garijo et al., 2009; Shlevkov and Morata, 2012; Wells et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on undead cells.

claim: Egr,p35-coexpressing cells completely arrest in G2.
source: Egr,p35-coexpressing cells completely arrest in G2 (Figure 7N), confirming that G2-stalling is intimately associated with cellular states known to stimulate non-autonomous growth.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7N by FUCCI analysis.

claim: G2-stalling is intimately associated with cellular states known to stimulate non-autonomous growth.
source: Egr,p35-coexpressing cells completely arrest in G2 (Figure 7N), confirming that G2-stalling is intimately associated with cellular states known to stimulate non-autonomous growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the complete G2 arrest in undead cells.

claim: The initiator caspase Dronc is required to stimulate non-autonomous growth from dying and undead cells.
source: Genetically, the initiator caspase Dronc is required to stimulate non-autonomous growth from dying and undead cells (Enomoto et al., 2015; Fan and Bergmann, 2008a; Fan and Bergmann, 2008b; Kiyokawa and Ray, 2008; Kondo et al., 2006; Wells et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on Dronc and non-autonomous growth.

claim: 24 hr after surgical injury, many CasExpress-positive clones were observed near the wound site.
source: Strikingly, 24 hr after surgical injury, we observed many CasExpress-positive clones near the wound site (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B by CasExpress analysis.

claim: Many wound-proximal cells survive caspase activation and subsequently proliferate.
source: This indicates that many wound-proximal cells survive caspase activation and subsequently proliferate.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of CasExpress-positive clones near the wound site.

claim: All SASP-like markers, including cell size, were highly elevated in egr-expressing discs.
source: As expected from many studies previously linking upregulation of these markers to JNK (Bunker et al., 2015; Fulda et al., 2010; Richardson and Portela, 2018; Santabárbara-Ruiz et al., 2015; Takino et al., 2014; Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006), we found all SASP-like markers, including cell size (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), to be highly elevated (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C-J).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C-J by analysis of upd-LacZ, MMP1, GstD-GFP, and Xbp1-GFP.

claim: The co-occurrence of G2-arrest, JNK activity and SASP-like markers suggests that a JNK-signaling induced G2-arrest in flies is linked to senescence-like phenotypes driven by JNK.
source: The co-occurrence of G2-arrest, JNK activity and SASP-like markers suggests that a JNK-signaling induced G2-arrest in flies is linked to senescence-like phenotypes driven by JNK.
evidence: This is inferred from the simultaneous presence of G2-arrest, JNK activity, and SASP markers.

claim: Transient upd-LacZ and MMP1 upregulation is associated with transient JNK activity in surgical injuries.
source: Importantly, transient upd-LacZ and MMP1 upregulation is associated with transient JNK activity in surgical injuries (Lin et al., 2010; McClure et al., 2008), making it plausible that transient G2-stalling is linked to senescence-like properties promoting wound healing and regeneration, analogous to senescent cells observed in a mammalian wound model (Demaria et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on upd and MMP1 in wound healing.

claim: JNK signaling induces a dose-dependent extension of G2, which results in either transient stalling or prolonged arrest of cells in G2.
source: Here we uncover a mechanism whereby control of the cell cycle promotes survival and mitogenic signaling in JNK-dependent responses to tissue stress. We demonstrate that JNK signaling induces a dose-dependent extension of G2, which results in either transient stalling or prolonged arrest of cells in G2.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cells in G2 are protected from undergoing JNK-induced apoptosis.
source: Cells in G2 are protected from undergoing JNK-induced apoptosis and promote proliferative signaling to the surrounding tissue in a SASP-like manner (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of findings demonstrated in Figure 6 and throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cells in G2 promote proliferative signaling to the surrounding tissue in a SASP-like manner.
source: Cells in G2 are protected from undergoing JNK-induced apoptosis and promote proliferative signaling to the surrounding tissue in a SASP-like manner (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of findings demonstrated in Figure 7 and throughout the manuscript.

claim: Any length of G2-stalling protects cells autonomously from JNK-induced apoptosis in G1.
source: Our data support a model where any length of G2-stalling protects cells autonomously from JNK-induced apoptosis in G1.
evidence: This is a model based on the apoptosis protection observed in G2-stalled cells.

claim: Stalled cells switch on a SASP-like phenotype, which when transient supports compensatory growth during regeneration.
source: Stalled cells switch on a SASP-like phenotype, which when transient supports compensatory growth during regeneration.
evidence: This is a model based on the transient G2-stalling and SASP markers observed in surgical injury.

claim: When cells stall chronically, proliferation is autonomously inhibited and chronic SASP-like phenotype drives non-autonomous overgrowth contributing to tumorigenesis.
source: However, when cells stall chronically, proliferation is autonomously inhibited and chronic SASP-like phenotype drives non-autonomous overgrowth contributing to tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a model based on the chronic G2-stalling observed in tumor models and its effects on non-autonomous growth.

claim: The spectrum of cell-autonomous and non-autonomous functions of G2-stalling is defined by the intensity and length of JNK activity.
source: We suggest that our experimental models reveal a spectrum of cell-autonomous (survival, stalling of proliferation) and non-autonomous (mitogenic paracrine signaling) functions of G2-stalling. Importantly, this spectrum is defined by the intensity and length of JNK activity: whereas persistent stalling of tumor cells may cause persistent survival and non-autonomous overgrowth, transient stalling of wound site cells may promote survival transiently and facilitate transient induction of compensatory proliferation.
evidence: This is a model integrating the findings from different experimental models with varying JNK activity levels and durations.

claim: Both G2-stalling and survival as well as apoptosis directly link to JNK signaling in response to tissue stress.
source: Surprisingly, both G2-stalling and survival as well as apoptosis directly link to JNK signaling in response to tissue stress.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the regulation of multiple pathways by JNK shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: JNK controls stg/cdc25 transcription and Trbl availability as rate-limiting factors for stalling.
source: We find that JNK controls stg/cdc25 transcription and Trbl availability as rate-limiting factors for stalling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by stg-GFP and Trbl-GFP reporter analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Mouse JNK directly phosphorylates Cdc25C to stall G2/M transitions.
source: Importantly, mouse JNK directly phosphorylates Cdc25C to stall G2/M transitions (Goss et al., 2003; Gutierrez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on mammalian JNK and Cdc25C.

claim: JNK regulates hid promoting apoptosis.
source: As reported before, JNK also regulates hid promoting apoptosis (Shlevkov and Morata, 2012) and activates Hippo/Yorkie promoting survival by upregulation of Diap1 (Sun and Irvine, 2011; Sun and Irvine, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and confirmed by Hid-GFP analysis in Figure 6.

claim: JNK activates Hippo/Yorkie promoting survival by upregulation of Diap1.
source: As reported before, JNK also regulates hid promoting apoptosis (Shlevkov and Morata, 2012) and activates Hippo/Yorkie promoting survival by upregulation of Diap1 (Sun and Irvine, 2011; Sun and Irvine, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and confirmed by Diap1-GFP analysis in Figure 6.

claim: Cell cycle progression from G2 to G1 represents the switch between anti- and pro-apoptotic activity of JNK.
source: However, the switch between the anti- and pro-apoptotic consequences are not understood (Fulda et al., 2010). Importantly, our observations imply that cell cycle progression from G2 to G1 represents the switch between anti- and pro-apoptotic activity of JNK.
evidence: This is a model based on the cell cycle phase-specific apoptosis patterns observed.

claim: G2-stalling is a protected state, which is dominated by pre-emptive protection from ROS damage through upregulation of the UPR, redox response and other repair pathways.
source: We suggest that stalling the cell cycle is a protected state, which is dominated by pre-emptive protection from ROS damage through upregulation of the UPR, redox response and other repair pathways.
evidence: This is a model based on the upregulation of stress response markers in G2-stalled cells.

claim: G2-stalling is important to keep the pro-apoptotic branch of JNK signaling suppressed, a prerequisite of efficient regeneration.
source: Thus, G2-stalling is important to keep the pro-apoptotic branch of JNK signaling suppressed, a prerequisite of efficient regeneration (La Fortezza et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a model based on the apoptosis protection in G2 and is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: G2-stalling is induced by JNK itself, and thus only indirectly by cellular damage.
source: We propose that G2-stalling is induced by JNK itself, and thus only indirectly by cellular damage.
evidence: This is a model based on the sufficiency and necessity of JNK for G2-stalling and the lack of requirement for DNA damage.

claim: Despite the fact that many JNK-signaling cells die in G1 when bypassing stalling in G2, there are many JNK-signaling G1 cells which survive, continue to cycle and are healthy enough to contribute to future adult tissues.
source: This indicates that, despite the fact that many JNK-signaling cells die in G1 when bypassing stalling in G2, there are many JNK-signaling G1 cells, which survive, continue to cycle and are healthy enough to contribute to future adult tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the improved regeneration when stg is overexpressed in egr-expressing discs.

claim: Developmentally regulated G2-stalling in the wing peripodium is dependent on JNK.
source: Even more strikingly, we find that independent of any tissue damage, developmentally regulated G2-stalling in the wing peripodium is dependent on JNK.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reduction in G2 cells in hepR75 mutant peripodium shown in Figure 3.

claim: Programmed cell arrest and senescence in mouse embryogenesis is independent of DNA damage or p53, but dependent on a general CDK-inhibitor (p21) and developmental signals of the TGF-β/SMAD or PI3K/FOXO pathways.
source: Similarly, programmed cell arrest and senescence in mouse embryogenesis is independent of DNA damage or p53, but dependent on a general CDK-inhibitor (p21) and developmental signals of the TGF-β/SMAD or PI3K/FOXO pathways (Davaapil et al., 2017; Muñoz-Espín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on developmental senescence in mammals.

claim: Cell cycle stalling and consequently, SASP or protection from apoptosis, may be under the control of signaling pathways which not always depend on tissue stress.
source: Thus, cell cycle stalling and consequently, SASP or protection from apoptosis, may be under the control of signaling pathways which not always depend on tissue stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental G2-stalling observed in the peripodium and developmental senescence in mammals.

claim: Another developmentally regulated G2 arrest has been reported to suppress apoptosis.
source: Curiously, another developmentally regulated G2 arrest has already been reported to suppress apoptosis (Qi and Calvi, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: At least one previous study has indicated the existence of senescent cells in flies, however their cell cycle stage was less well-defined.
source: At least one previous study has indicated the existence of senescent cells in flies, however their cell cycle stage was less well-defined (Nakamura et al., 2014; Neves et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on senescence in flies.

claim: Many studies have demonstrated correlation of JNK with SASP-like characteristics in flies, such as mitogenic signaling, ECM remodeling or ROS production.
source: Many studies have demonstrated correlation of JNK with SASP-like characteristics in flies, such as mitogenic signaling, ECM remodeling or ROS production (Brock et al., 2017; Khan et al., 2017; McClure et al., 2008; Nakamura et al., 2014; Neves et al., 2015; Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2013; Ryoo et al., 2004; Uhlirova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on JNK and SASP-like features.

claim: G2-stalling may either represent a primitive version of a senescent cell cycle arrest that evolved to G0 in mammalian cells or that G2-stalling may also occur in mammals but is less well-defined.
source: We speculate that G2-stalling may either represent a primitive version of a senescent cell cycle arrest that evolved to G0 in mammalian cells or that G2-stalling may also occur in mammals but is less well-defined.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary relationship between G2-stalling in flies and senescence in mammals.

claim: Recent studies implicate a role for cells with senescent markers in mammalian wounds and vertebrate development.
source: Recent studies implicate a role for cells with senescent markers in mammalian wounds and vertebrate development (Davaapil et al., 2017; Demaria et al., 2014; Muñoz-Espín et al., 2013; Ritschka et al., 2017) and an injury-induced G2 arrest has been found to interfere with restoration of epithelial homeostasis in a model of chronic kidney disease (Bonventre, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on senescence in mammalian tissues.

claim: An injury-induced G2 arrest has been found to interfere with restoration of epithelial homeostasis in a model of chronic kidney disease.
source: Recent studies implicate a role for cells with senescent markers in mammalian wounds and vertebrate development (Davaapil et al., 2017; Demaria et al., 2014; Muñoz-Espín et al., 2013; Ritschka et al., 2017) and an injury-induced G2 arrest has been found to interfere with restoration of epithelial homeostasis in a model of chronic kidney disease (Bonventre, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study on kidney disease.

claim: G2-stalling may offer an opportunity to protect cells from apoptosis, induce paracrine signals and, importantly, restore active cycling upon restoration of tissue homeostasis, instead of engaging permanent senescence in G0.
source: G2-stalling may offer an opportunity to protect cells from apoptosis, induce paracrine signals and, importantly, restore active cycling upon restoration of tissue homeostasis, instead of engaging permanent senescence in G0.
evidence: This is a model based on the reversible nature of G2-stalling and its functional consequences.
